query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: The formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide scale in CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high‐entropy alloys is primarily governed by a synergistic effect between chromium and aluminum when they are homogeneously distributed in a single-phase solid solution. In this state, controlled outward diffusion of Cr and Al during high-temperature exposure (>900 °C) promotes the nucleation and growth of a continuous (Cr,Al)2O3-type scale that resists crack formation and spallation. In contrast, when the alloy is multiphase with elemental segregation, competing oxidation reactions (e.g., formation of Mn-, or mixed oxide phases) occur at localized regions, leading to heterogeneous oxide scale growth, stress concentrations, and eventual spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy with X as Si, Mn, or Al in either a single-phase, homogeneous solid solution or a multiphase, chemically segregated structure.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C (both isothermal and cyclic exposures) while monitoring in situ oxide phase evolution and microstructural changes.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (≥900 °C) in oxygen-rich (or corrosive) environments; comparisons between samples with single-phase versus controlled multiphase microstructures; variations in X (Si, Mn, or Al) content.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of phase homogeneity and the local concentration of Cr and Al, which together mediate the ability to form a uniform, coherent (Cr,Al)2O3 protective oxide.
generation.mechanism: In homogeneous, single-phase alloys, synchronized outward diffusion of Cr and Al at elevated temperatures leads to the nucleation of a slow-growing, adherent (Cr,Al)2O3 scale that minimizes internal stresses. In multiphase alloys, elemental segregation causes localized variations in oxidation kinetics, promoting the formation of mixed oxide phases (e.g., Mn-oxides or Si-oxides) that produce uneven growth, internal stress, and cracking/spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with a single-phase, Cr- and Al-rich microstructure (especially when X = Al) will develop a thin, coherent, and adherent (Cr,Al)2O3 oxide layer that persists under prolonged exposure at >900 °C. In contrast, samples exhibiting multiphase microstructures with significant elemental segregation (or with X = Si or Mn) will form heterogeneous oxide layers that exhibit cracking and spallation, resulting in poorer oxidation and corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: A standard NiCr-based alloy known to form protective chromia scales under similar conditions, to serve as a reference for oxide coherence and adherence.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys operating in industrially relevant high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidative or corrosive environments, and it is specifically relevant to alloys in which the phase state (single-phase vs. multiphase) can be controlled via processing.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale formation and the role of minor alloying elements or trace impurities in modifying diffusion pathways remain uncertain. Additionally, the transition conditions between cohesive and non-cohesive oxide formation in marginal multiphase microstructures may vary depending on processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX samples (with X = Al and with X = Mn or Si) processed to exhibit either a single-phase homogeneous microstructure or a controlled multiphase, segregated microstructure. Expose all samples to an oxidative atmosphere at ≥950 °C under both isothermal and cyclic conditions. Use in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to monitor oxide formation, scale coherence, and microstructure evolution. A NiCr-based alloy should be used as a baseline control.
measurements: In situ XRD to track oxide phase formation and growth kinetics
TEM/SEM cross-sectional imaging to assess oxide scale thickness, continuity, and interface quality
EDS mapping for local elemental distributions across scale and substrate
Weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation kinetics
Spallation and crack propagation evaluations during cyclic exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both single-phase and multiphase samples, regardless of X (Al, Si, or Mn), form similarly coherent, crack-free oxide scales with oxidation resistance comparable to the baseline NiCr alloy under the same conditions, then the hypothesis that local Cr-Al synergy and microstructural homogeneity govern protective oxide formation is falsified.

Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. decision.trend: A recent study on the oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (PMC9498035) uses computational approaches to show that stable oxide-scale formation strongly depends on local composition and phase distribution, particularly the presence of Al and Cr. The work suggests that if the alloy remains single-phase or maintains controlled phase boundaries, a continuous (Cr,Al)2O3-type scale can form without severe spallation. However, in multiphase microstructures with strong elemental segregation, different oxide products can separate laterally, weakening the protective layer and causing spallation. While modeling predicts critical roles for chemistry and microstructure on oxide stability, conclusive experimental demonstration at temperatures above 900 °C remains an open challenge, especially under cyclic or complex corrosive conditions.
decision.unsolved: It is still not definitively established how to ensure a stable and crack-free scale forms and persists at elevated temperatures in CrFeCoNiX (X=Si, Mn, or Al) HEAs. Key issues include whether the synergy of Cr-Al content in controlling (Cr,Al)2O3-type scales is sufficient in real service environments and how phase boundaries or short-range ordering may alter oxide nucleation and spallation resistance.
decision.lever: Conduct high-temperature (≥900 °C) environmental X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy experiments on well-controlled single-phase versus multiphase CrFeCoNiX samples (varying X among Si, Mn, Al) in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres. Use a standard NiCr-based alloy as a baseline comparison, and systematically track oxide layer growth, composition, and cracking/spallation behavior during isothermal and cyclic exposures.
decision.why: In-situ characterization under realistic high-temperature conditions directly tests whether coherent, protective (Cr,Al)2O3 or other stable oxide phases form and remain adherent. Prior modeling (PMC9498035) indicates that controlled local composition and phase distribution in Al-rich CrFeCoNiX alloys can produce protective oxide scales, but this has not been conclusively validated. A falsifying observation would be the development of non-protective, spalling oxide films even under carefully controlled Cr-Al conditions, contradicting the hypothesis that coherent oxide formation is governed primarily by the synergy of local Cr/Al content and single-phase or mild multiphase microstructures.
